legacy_report:
SOURCE: "End-To-End Memory Networks", Sainbayar Sukhbaatar, Arthur Szlam, Jason Weston, Rob Fergus (NYU / Facebook AI Research). Published at NeurIPS (NIPS) 2015. The PDF is arXiv:1503.08895v5, dated 24 Nov 2015.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/02-context-engineering/sources/sukhbaatar-2015-end-end-memory-networks.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 11 of 11 pages, 47,313 of 47,313 chars, page markers included. That covers the body (pp.1-8), the references (p.9), Appendix A with the 10k results table (p.10) and Appendix B with the attention visualisations (p.11). Nothing was skipped. I skimmed the references only for origins.

CORE MECHANISM (pp.1-3)
- **Soft attention over memory.** Each input sentence x_i is embedded with matrix A to give a memory vector m_i. The query is embedded with B to give u. The attention weight is "pi = Softmax(uTmi). (1)" (p.2). Each slot also has an output vector c_i (matrix C). The read is "o = ∑i pici. (2)" (p.2). The answer is "ˆa = Softmax(W (o +u)) (3)" (p.2). "Because the function from input to output is smooth, we can easily compute gradients and back-propagate through it." (p.2)
- **Multiple hops.** Hops are stacked as "uk+1 =uk +ok. (4)" (p.2). The paper says the model is "similar to the Memory Network model in [23], except that the hard max operations within each layer have been replaced with a continuous weighting from the softmax." (p.3)
- **Weight tying, two schemes (p.3).**
  - "Adjacent: the output embedding for one layer is the input embedding for the one above, i.e.Ak+1 = C k", plus W^T = C_K and B = A_1.
  - "Layer-wise (RNN-like): the input and output embeddings are the same across different layers", with an added linear map "uk+1 =Hu k +ok". With layer-wise tying the model "can be cast as a traditional RNN" whose recurrence is over hops rather than over the text.
- **Temporal encoding (p.5).** "mi = ∑jAxij + TA(i), where TA(i) is the ith row of a special matrix TA that encodes temporal information". It is learned. "sentences are indexed in reverse order, reflecting their relative distance from the question".
- **Random noise, RN (p.5).** "at training time we can randomly add 10% of empty memories to the stories".
- **Position encoding, PE (pp.4-5).** Each word embedding is weighted by l_kj = (1−j/J) − (k/d)(1−2j/J), so word order affects m_i. Bag-of-words "cannot capture the order of the words in the sentence".

CLAIMS

1. Without supporting-fact supervision, the end-to-end model gets close to strongly supervised MemNN but still trails it.
   - number: 1k: 6.7% vs 12.6% mean error. 10k: 3.2% vs 4.2%.
   - setup: bAbI v1.1, 20 tasks, vocabulary V=177. MemN2N with PE + LS + RN, K=3 hops, adjacent tying. 1k runs are trained jointly on all tasks (d=50). The 10k number comes from a larger d=100 model with a ReLU after each hop, trained per task (Table 3, column RN*).
   - quote: "1k: 6.7% for MemNN vs 12.6% for MemN2N with position encoding + linear start + random noise, jointly trained and 10k: 3.2% for MemNN vs 4.2% for MemN2N with position encoding + linear start + random noise + non-linearity4, although the supervised models are still superior."
   - where: p.6, §4.4

2. Failed-task counts (error > 5%) give the same picture.
   - number: 4 failed tasks (MemNN) vs 11 (best MemN2N) at 1k. 2 vs 3 at 10k.
   - setup: Table 1 (1k) and Table 3 (10k, RN* column).
   - quote: "Failed tasks (err. > 5%) 4 20 18 15 13 12 11 17 11 11 11 10" (p.6) and "Failed tasks (err. > 5%) 2 16 17 9 6 4 4 3 16 7 6 6 6" (p.10)

3. More hops reduce QA error.
   - number: 1k mean error is 25.8% with 1 hop, 15.6% with 2, 13.3% with 3. 10k: 24.5%, 10.9%, 7.9%.
   - setup: PE + LS, joint training (the "1 hop / 2 hops / 3 hops PE LS joint" columns).
   - quote: "Importantly, more computational hops give improved performance." (p.6). Table rows: "Mean error (%) 6.7 51.3 40.2 25.1 20.3 16.3 13.9 25.8 15.6 13.3 12.4 15.2" and "Mean error (%) 3.2 36.4 39.2 15.4 9.4 7.2 6.6 24.5 10.9 7.9 7.5 11.0" (columns 8-10 are 1, 2 and 3 hops).
   - where: p.6, Table 1

4. Every MemN2N variant beats the weakly supervised baselines.
   - number: LSTM 51.3% and MemNN-WSH 40.2% mean error at 1k.
   - setup: same 1k table. The baselines see only question/answer pairs.
   - quote: "All variants of our proposed model comfortably beat the weakly supervised baseline methods."
   - where: p.6

5. Linear start (removing the softmaxes early in training) helps avoid local minima.
   - number: 53.6% → 1.6% error on task 16.
   - setup: bAbI 1k, per-task training.
   - quote: "See task 16 in Table 1, where PE alone gets 53.6% error, while using LS reduces it to 1.6%."
   - where: p.6
   - note: the printed Table 1 shows 52.1 for PE on task 16. The prose says 53.6. This is an internal inconsistency in the paper.

6. On language modelling, MemN2N gets slightly lower perplexity than tuned RNN/SCRN/LSTM baselines.
   - number: Penn Treebank 111 vs 115. Text8 147 vs 154.
   - setup: PTB has 929k/73k/82k words and a 10k vocabulary; the best run is 150 hidden, 7 hops, memory 200. Text8 has a ~44k vocabulary; the best run is 500 hidden, 7 hops, memory 100. Each memory cell holds one word, the query is a constant 0.1, tying is layer-wise and ReLU is applied to half the units. Baselines come from Mikolov et al. [15].
   - quote: "Our MemN2N approach achieves lower perplexity on both datasets (111 vs 115 for RNN/SCRN on Penn and 147 vs 154 for LSTM on Text8)."
   - where: p.8, §5.2; Table 2, p.7

7. More hops also help language modelling.
   - number: PTB test perplexity goes from 121 at 2 hops to 114 at 7 hops. Text8 goes from 187 to 147. Memory size is 100 in both.
   - quote: rows "MemN2N 150 2 100 128 121 500 2 100 152 187" and "150 7 100 120 114 500 7 100 118 147"; caption "Note that increasing the number of memory hops improves performance."
   - where: p.7, Table 2

8. Parameter count differs across the compared models.
   - number: ~1.5x for MemN2N, ~4x for LSTM, each relative to an RNN with the same hidden units.
   - quote: "MemN2N has∼1.5x more parameters than RNNs with the same number of hidden units, while LSTM has ∼4x more parameters."
   - where: p.8

9. The hops specialise in language modelling. Some attend to recent words, others spread over the whole memory, and the two types alternate. Attention does not decay with distance.
   - number: none
   - quote: "some hops concentrate only on recent words, while other hops have more broad attention over all memory locations ... unlike a traditional RNN, the cache does not decay exponentially: it has roughly the same average activation across the entire memory."
   - where: p.8

10. Even without supporting-fact labels, the model learns to attend to the right supporting sentences on most tasks.
    - number: none
    - quote: "MemN2N successfully learns to focus on the correct supporting sentences."
    - where: Fig. 2 caption, p.7; Fig. 4, p.11

11. Memory capacity is bounded in the QA setup.
    - number: 50 sentences in the window; up to 320 sentences per story.
    - quote: "The capacity of memory is restricted to the most recent 50 sentences." (p.5) and "a set of I sentences{xi} whereI≤ 320" (p.4)

12. Results are sensitive to initialisation, and the paper picks the best of 10 runs by training error.
    - number: 10 restarts.
    - quote: "we repeated each training 10 times with different random initializations, and picked the one with the lowest training error."
    - where: p.5

LIMITS
- The authors concede three points:
  - "Our model is still unable to exactly match the performance of the memory networks trained with strong supervision, and both fail on several of the 1k QA tasks." (p.8)
  - "smooth lookups may not scale well to the case where a larger memory is required. For these settings, we plan to explore multiscale notions of attention or hashing" (p.8)
  - Text8 had "only a single training run ... due to limited time constraints" (p.8).
- Persistent failures: task 19 (path finding) is at 82.8-100% error at 1k, and task 17 (positional reasoning) at ~40-51%. Both are fixed at 10k only by the larger non-linear RN* model (2.3% and 18.6%).
- What it does not show:
  - The memory is tiny: 50 sentences for QA, at most 200 words for language modelling.
  - The QA data is synthetic with a 177-word vocabulary.
  - No compute or latency cost is reported.
  - There is no write or update policy. Memory is all inputs written sequentially, up to a buffer.
  - There is no retrieval over large external stores.
- Dated aspects: the language-modelling baselines are 2014 RNN/LSTM models; this predates the Transformer. Best-of-10 selection on training error inflates the reported numbers.
- For the course: this is soft attention over an in-model memory of a few dozen items. It is not evidence about LLM context windows or retrieval at scale.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Weston, Chopra, Bordes, "Memory networks", ICLR 2015 [23]. This is the hard-max, strongly supervised predecessor; MemN2N is "a continuous form of the Memory Network".
- Bahdanau, Cho, Bengio, ICLR 2015 [2], "RNNsearch". MemN2N is described as "an extension of RNNsearch [2] to the case where multiple computational steps (hops) are performed per output symbol". The differences: Bahdanau attends over a single sentence and scores with a gated network, where MemN2N scores with a simple linear/inner product.
- Graves, Wayne, Danihelka, "Neural turing machines", 2014 [8]. NTM uses content and address access; MemN2N uses content only, with temporal features giving "a kind of address-based access". It needs no sharpening because it writes sequentially.
- Weston, Bordes, Chopra, Mikolov 2015 [22], the bAbI tasks.
- Mikolov et al. 2014 [15] for the language-modelling baselines and data.
- Peng et al. 2015 [17] for the non-linearity that fixes tasks 17 and 19.
- Early nearest-neighbour memories: Steinbuch and Piske 1963 [19], Taylor 1959 [21].
- Xu et al. 2015 [24] (Show, Attend and Tell).
- Goodman 2001 [6] (n-gram plus cache).

CODE
- No code in the paper. Footnote, p.5: "MemN2N source code is available at https://github.com/facebook/MemNN."
- Load-bearing equations, verbatim from p.2: "pi = Softmax(uTmi). (1)", "o = ∑i pici. (2)", "ˆa = Softmax(W (o +u)) (3)", "uk+1 =uk +ok. (4)".

FIGURES
- **Figure 1, p.2 (best candidate for the mechanism):** "(a): A single layer version of our model. (b): A three layer version of our model. In practice, we can constrain several of the embedding matrices to be the same (see Section 2.2)." One diagram shows query → inner product with memory → softmax → weighted sum → hop stacking. That is faster than reading the equations.
- **Figure 2, p.7 (candidate for multi-hop reads):** "Example predictions on the QA tasks of [22]. We show the labeled supporting facts (support) from the dataset which MemN2N does not use during training, and the probabilities p of each hop used by the model during inference." It shows concretely that hop 1 and hop 3 pick different supporting sentences. For example, on the 2-supporting-facts story, "John took the milk there" gets 0.88/1.00 in hops 1-2, then "John moved to the hallway" gets 1.00 in hop 3.
- **Figure 3, p.7:** "Average activation weight of memory positions during 6 memory hops." It shows the recent-word hops alternating with the broad-attention hops in language modelling. This is useful for a "cache that does not decay" point.
- **Figure 4, p.11:** the attention weights for all 20 tasks, with errors marked in red.

PROBLEMS
- The text extracted cleanly.
- pypdf warned about a missing fontTools. There was no visible damage, apart from some dropped spaces in equations (e.g. "uTmi").
- The tables extract as space-separated rows. I mapped the column headers by order; they are consistent with the prose.
- Table 3 prints "18,6" with a comma for task 17 in the RN* column. This is a typo in the source.
- The PE-on-task-16 figure disagrees between prose (53.6) and Table 1 (52.1), as noted under claim 5.
- Figure 3 is an image; only its caption extracts.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
